message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This proposal is built on our own trading history, not just competitor benchmarking, and that is what makes me confident in it. The key question with any rate rise is price sensitivity, and we have a direct test: when we raised the weekend rate by £10 last June, weekend occupancy went up, from 81% to 89%, the following month. Combined with a value-for-money score of 8.4, the best in our set, and rates £20 to £35 below competitors, everything points the same way. The revenue estimate is deliberately conservative: it assumes no occupancy gain and puts no value at all on the extra Friday and Sunday nights that the two-night minimum will generate, so £204,000 is a floor rather than a target. We have also built in a clear monitoring trigger, so if occupancy does dip we will see it within a month and can respond. Corporate and group commitments are protected. I think this is a well-evidenced, low-risk change that brings our pricing into line with the quality of the hotel.
</author>

<document>
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.
</document>
response:
# Review: Weekend Rate Restructure

The core idea is defensible. You are priced below every competitor, and a £20 rise still leaves you level with the cheapest. But the key evidence on price sensitivity doesn't show what the paper claims, the revenue figure uses the wrong room count and overstates what a BAR increase can capture, and the two-night minimum conflicts with your own wedding data.

## 1. The June–July "test" doesn't measure price sensitivity

The occupancy rise from 81% in June to 89% in July coincides with the period that section 2 itself names as your strongest: **the harbour festival and the school summer holidays**. July and August are high every year, and the rate rise and the seasonal peak happened together. Two further points:
- June 2025 (81%) was *below* May (85%), so June was a soft month, which makes the jump look larger.
- There's no comparison with July 2024, or with competitors in the same months.

A seasonal rise explains the jump with no help from the price change. The rise tells you nothing about price sensitivity either way, and certainly not that the higher rate "reinforced our positioning."

**A better test:** compare the change in occupancy from 2024 to 2025 by month, before and after the rise. Or look at booking pace and how quickly you sold out in the weeks after the change against the same weeks a year earlier.

The value-for-money score of 8.4 is a genuine positive, but it was measured at **£145**. It shows guests feel well served at that price, not that they'll feel the same at £165.

## 2. The revenue figure uses the wrong room count and overstates what's captured

**The room count.** Section 2 says the hotel has **112 rooms**. The revenue calculation uses **124**:
- 124 × 104 × 79% × £20 = **£203,800**
- 112 × 104 × 79% × £20 = **£184,000**

**Not every room pays BAR.** The calculation applies £20 to every occupied weekend room, but the increase only reaches rooms sold at BAR or rates linked to it:
- **Wedding and group blocks**, about **38% of Saturday rooms**, are booked at group rates and won't pick up the rise, especially those already contracted.
- **Corporate contracted rates** are explicitly honoured, though they're a small share of weekend business.
- **OTA bookings** pay commission, often 15–20%, so net revenue per room is lower.
- **Packages and promotions** may not move in step with BAR.

**Year one will be lower.** By 1 June, much of summer 2026, your peak, will already be booked at £145. The £184,000 is a full-year, steady-state figure at best.

Taken together, a realistic gain is probably well below £184,000, even before any volume loss. Calling the figure "a floor rather than a target", as your summary does, isn't supported. It rests on an assumption of no lost occupancy, and section 1 shows that assumption has no evidence behind it.

**A useful point to add.** At £165, revenue only falls below today's level if occupancy drops by about **12%**, which means from 79% to roughly **69–70%**. That margin is a real strength of the proposal and gives the case its strongest footing. Your five-point monitoring trigger sits sensibly inside that margin.

## 3. The two-night minimum conflicts with your wedding business

Section 4 says weddings account for **about 38% of Saturday bookings**, and that these guests **arrive on Saturday and leave on Sunday**, one night only. A two-night minimum on every stay including a Saturday would either:
- **apply to wedding blocks**, putting at risk a large share of your Saturday trade and your relationship with Quayside Hall, or
- **exempt them**, in which case the policy only affects the remaining ~62% of Saturday guests, and the paper should say so.

**Other risks:**
- On the **31 sold-out Saturdays**, a minimum stay makes sense, because demand exceeds supply. On the other **~21 Saturdays**, it may turn away guests who only want one night, so you would *lose* revenue.
- The paper assumes single-night guests will convert to two nights. Some will simply book a competitor instead.

So the minimum stay isn't a guaranteed upside, as your summary treats it. Its value could be negative. Consider applying it only to high-demand dates, the sold-out and near-sold-out Saturdays, with wedding blocks clearly exempted.

## 4. Monitoring

The five-point trigger is sensible and well within the break-even margin. Two refinements:
- **Watch booking pace, not just occupancy.** Because guests book weeks or months ahead, a problem shows up in forward bookings long before it shows in monthly occupancy. Weekly pick-up against 2025 does this, so make it the main measure.
- **Separate the two changes.** If occupancy falls, you won't know whether the rate or the minimum stay caused it. Introducing them at different times, or the minimum stay on selected dates only, would let you tell.

## 5. Checks that are correct

- **Average 2025 occupancy:** 79.2% ✓
- **Competitor gap:** £20–35 ✓. At £165 you'd match the cheapest competitor.
- **Weekend nights:** 52 × 2 = 104 ✓
- **Contracted corporate and group rates are honoured** ✓

## Your summary against the document

| Claim | Status |
|---|---|
| Direct test of price sensitivity | ✗ Confounded by the July peak |
| Value score 8.4, rates below competitors | ✓, but measured at £145 |
| £204,000 is a floor | ✗ About £184k with the correct room count, less after group, OTA and pre-booked rooms, with no evidence for holding volume |
| Minimum stay is pure upside | ✗ Conflicts with wedding trade and may lose single-night bookings |
| Monitoring trigger | ✓ Sensible. Lead with booking pace |
| Corporate and group protected | ✓ |

## Suggested revisions

1. Replace the June–July evidence with a year-on-year comparison, or describe the price sensitivity as untested.
2. Use 112 rooms, and apply the £20 only to BAR-linked rooms, net of OTA commission. Show year one separately.
3. Add the break-even analysis (about 69–70% occupancy). It's the strongest argument you have.
4. Exempt wedding and group blocks from the minimum stay, and limit it to high-demand dates.
5. Make booking pace the primary monitoring measure, and consider staggering the two changes.

On those terms, a more modest gain, probably in the low-to-mid six figures if volume holds, is still a sound case.
